subject: physics
overview: This unit covers repetitive motion, from simple harmonic motion of springs and pendulums to mechanical waves on strings and in air columns, including superposition, standing waves and beats. NEET asks 2-3 questions from it almost every year, mostly on SHM equations and energy, time periods of oscillating systems, wave equations, organ pipe and string harmonics, and beats. Questions are formula-driven but often hide a conceptual twist.

topics.explanation: A motion that repeats itself after equal intervals of time is periodic motion. Examples are the Earth's revolution, a clock's hands and a swinging pendulum. If a body moves to and fro about a fixed mean (equilibrium) position, the periodic motion is called oscillatory or vibratory. Every oscillation is periodic, but not every periodic motion is oscillatory; uniform circular motion is periodic but not to and fro. The time period $T$ is the smallest interval after which the motion repeats, measured in seconds. Frequency $\nu$ is the number of repetitions per second, with unit hertz (Hz). Angular frequency is $\omega = 2\pi\nu$ in rad/s. The state of the body at any instant is described by its displacement $x(t)$ from the mean position. Displacement may be linear, angular, a pressure change or an electric field, depending on the system.
key_points: Periodic motion repeats after a fixed time T.
Oscillatory motion is periodic motion about a mean position.
All oscillations are periodic; the converse is not true.
Unit of frequency is Hz, equal to $s^{-1}$.
Displacement is measured from the equilibrium position, not from the extreme position.
topics.neet_tip: Expect statement-type questions that separate periodic motion from oscillatory motion, or simple T, ν, ω conversions.
topics.topic: Periodic motion: time period, frequency, displacement as a function of time

topics.explanation: A function $f(t)$ is periodic if $f(t+T) = f(t)$ for the smallest positive $T$, which is its period. The simplest periodic functions are $\sin\omega t$ and $\cos\omega t$, each with period $2\pi/\omega$. A linear combination $a\sin\omega t + b\cos\omega t$ is also periodic and is itself a simple harmonic function, with amplitude $\sqrt{a^2+b^2}$. Any periodic function can be expressed as a superposition of sines and cosines of different time periods with suitable coefficients. $\sin^2\omega t = \frac{1-\cos2\omega t}{2}$ is periodic with period $\pi/\omega$. It represents SHM about the mean value 1/2, with angular frequency $2\omega$. $\sin\omega t + \sin2\omega t$ is periodic but not SHM. Functions such as $e^{-\omega t}$ and $\log\omega t$ are non-periodic.
key_points: The condition for periodicity is $f(t+T)=f(t)$.
$\sin\omega t$ and $\cos\omega t$ both have period $2\pi/\omega$.
$a\sin\omega t + b\cos\omega t$ is SHM with amplitude $\sqrt{a^2+b^2}$.
$\sin^2\omega t$ and $\cos^2\omega t$ have period $\pi/\omega$.
A sum of sinusoids with different ω is periodic but not simple harmonic.
Exponential and logarithmic functions are non-periodic.

formulas.meaning: Combining two sinusoids of the same ω into a single SHM

topics.neet_tip: NEET lists functions and asks which are periodic, which are SHM, or what their period is.

topics.explanation: In simple harmonic motion (SHM), the acceleration is proportional to the displacement from the mean position and always directed towards it: $a = -\omega^2 x$. Its solution is $x = A\cos(\omega t+\phi)$. Here $A$ is the amplitude, the maximum displacement. $(\omega t+\phi)$ is the phase, which fixes position and direction of motion at time t. $\phi$ is the phase constant (initial phase). SHM is the projection of uniform circular motion on a diameter. Velocity is $v = -A\omega\sin(\omega t+\phi)$, with magnitude $\omega\sqrt{A^2-x^2}$. Velocity is maximum ($A\omega$) at the mean position and zero at the extremes. Acceleration is maximum ($A\omega^2$) at the extremes and zero at the mean position. Velocity leads displacement by $\pi/2$, and acceleration leads displacement by $\pi$.
key_points: Defining condition: $a \propto -x$, or $F = -kx$.
Phase determines the state of motion; phase constant is the phase at t = 0.
$v_{max} = A\omega$ at the mean position; $a_{max} = A\omega^2$ at the extremes.
The v-x graph is an ellipse; the a-x graph is a straight line of negative slope.
Time from mean to extreme is T/4; time from mean to A/2 is T/12.
Velocity and displacement are $90^\circ$ out of phase; acceleration and displacement are $180^\circ$ out of phase.

formulas.meaning: Ellipse in the x-v plane; it becomes a circle when $\omega = 1$

topics.neet_tip: Frequently tested items are the ratios $v_{max}/a_{max} = 1/\omega$, time to travel between two positions, and phase relations.
topics.topic: Simple harmonic motion, its equation and phase

topics.explanation: A mass m attached to an ideal spring experiences a restoring force $F = -kx$ (Hooke's law). The spring (force) constant $k$, in N/m, measures stiffness. This gives $\omega = \sqrt{k/m}$ and $T = 2\pi\sqrt{m/k}$, independent of amplitude. For a vertical spring, gravity only shifts the mean position, so T is unchanged and $T = 2\pi\sqrt{\Delta l/g}$, where $\Delta l$ is the static extension. For springs in series, $1/k = 1/k_1+1/k_2$; in parallel, $k = k_1+k_2$. When a spring is cut, $k \propto 1/l$, so each piece is stiffer. The general rule for any system is $T = 2\pi\sqrt{\text{inertia factor}/\text{restoring force per unit displacement}}$. For example, a floating cylinder of length L and density $\rho_c$ in a liquid of density $\rho_l$ has $T = 2\pi\sqrt{L\rho_c/(\rho_l g)}$, so $T \propto 1/\sqrt{\rho_l}$.
key_points: Restoring force is $F = -kx$; k has unit N/m.
T is independent of amplitude and of g for a spring-mass system.
Series combination gives a softer spring; parallel gives a stiffer one.
Cutting a spring into n equal parts makes each part's constant nk.
A floating body, liquid in a U-tube, and a ball in a tunnel through the Earth are all SHM by the same method.

formulas.meaning: Vertical spring with static extension $\Delta l$
Floating body, where h is the depth submerged at equilibrium

topics.neet_tip: Expect spring combinations, cut springs, and the 'derive T for an unusual system' type (cork in a liquid, U-tube).
topics.topic: Oscillations of a spring: restoring force and force constant

topics.explanation: In SHM, kinetic energy is $K = \frac{1}{2}m\omega^2(A^2-x^2)$ and potential energy is $U = \frac{1}{2}kx^2$. The total energy $E = \frac{1}{2}kA^2 = \frac{1}{2}m\omega^2A^2$ stays constant when there is no damping. K is maximum at the mean position; U is maximum at the extremes. Both K and U oscillate with frequency $2\nu$, that is, with period T/2, while the total stays fixed. Averaged over a cycle, $\langle K\rangle = \langle U\rangle = E/2$. K equals U at $x = A/\sqrt{2}$. The energy-position graphs are parabolas: U opens upward, K opens downward, and their sum is a horizontal line. Energy is proportional to the square of both the amplitude and the frequency.
key_points: Total energy is proportional to $A^2$ and to $\omega^2$.
K and U vary with period T/2.
K = U at $x = \pm A/\sqrt{2}$.
At x = A/2, K = 3E/4 and U = E/4.
Time-averaged K and U each equal E/2.
In the x-v plane the curve is an ellipse; it is a circle only if $\omega = 1$, that is, k = m numerically.
topics.neet_tip: Standard questions ask the fraction of energy as kinetic at a given x, the position where K = U, or the frequency of energy oscillation.
topics.topic: Energy in SHM: kinetic and potential energies

topics.explanation: A simple pendulum is a point mass hanging from a light, inextensible string of length l. The restoring torque is $-mgl\sin\theta$. For small angles, $\sin\theta \approx \theta$, so the motion is angular SHM with $T = 2\pi\sqrt{l/g}$. T is independent of the bob's mass and, for small amplitudes, of the amplitude. Here l is measured from the point of suspension to the centre of the bob. A seconds pendulum has T = 2 s and $l \approx 1$ m (about 0.99 m). In non-inertial frames, replace g by $g_{eff}$. In a lift accelerating up, $g_{eff} = g+a$; accelerating down, $g-a$; in free fall, $g_{eff} = 0$, so the pendulum does not oscillate. In a car accelerating horizontally, $g_{eff} = \sqrt{g^2+a^2}$. Raising temperature lengthens l, so the pendulum clock loses time. On the Moon, T is larger.
key_points: Valid only for small angular amplitude.
$T \propto \sqrt{l}$ and $T \propto 1/\sqrt{g}$; independent of mass.
Seconds pendulum: T = 2 s, l is about 1 m.
Use $g_{eff}$ in a lift, an accelerating car or a liquid medium.
A girl standing up on a swing raises the centre of mass, so l decreases and T decreases.

formulas.meaning: Period of a simple pendulum for small oscillations
Fractional change in period for a small change in length

topics.neet_tip: Common angles are g_eff in a lift or car, percentage change in T when l changes, and effect of mass or amplitude (none).
topics.topic: Simple pendulum and its time period

topics.explanation: A wave is a disturbance that transfers energy and momentum through a medium without net transport of matter. Each particle only oscillates about its mean position. Mechanical waves need a medium with elasticity and inertia. Electromagnetic waves need no medium. In a transverse wave, particles vibrate perpendicular to the direction of propagation, forming crests and troughs; examples are waves on a stretched string and EM waves. Transverse mechanical waves need shear rigidity, so they travel in solids and along strings but not through the bulk of fluids. In a longitudinal wave, particles vibrate along the direction of propagation, forming compressions and rarefactions; sound in air is the example. Longitudinal waves travel in solids, liquids and gases. Ripples on a water surface are a combination of both types.
key_points: Waves transport energy, not matter.
Transverse waves have crests and troughs; longitudinal waves have compressions and rarefactions.
Sound in gases is purely longitudinal.
Transverse mechanical waves cannot travel through the bulk of gases or liquids.
Polarisation is possible only for transverse waves.
Sound cannot travel in vacuum; light can.
topics.neet_tip: Assertion-reason or statement questions test the medium requirement, the nature of sound, and polarisation applying only to transverse waves.
topics.topic: Wave motion: longitudinal and transverse waves

topics.explanation: Wave speed is $v = \nu\lambda$. It depends on the medium's elastic and inertial properties, not on the source. When a wave passes into another medium, its frequency stays the same while speed and wavelength change. For a transverse wave on a string, $v = \sqrt{T/\mu}$, where T is tension and $\mu$ is mass per unit length. For longitudinal waves, $v = \sqrt{B/\rho}$ in fluids and $v = \sqrt{Y/\rho}$ in thin rods. Newton assumed isothermal compressions, $v = \sqrt{P/\rho}$, which gave about 280 m/s for air. Laplace corrected this to adiabatic compressions, $v = \sqrt{\gamma P/\rho}$, giving about 331 m/s at STP. At constant temperature, changing pressure does not change v, because $P/\rho$ stays constant. In gases, $v \propto \sqrt{T}$ and $v \propto 1/\sqrt{M}$. Humidity increases v, since moist air is less dense. In general, $v_{solid} > v_{liquid} > v_{gas}$.
key_points: Frequency is set by the source; speed is set by the medium.
String: $v \propto \sqrt{T}$.
Laplace correction: compressions in sound are adiabatic.
Pressure has no effect on v at constant temperature.
$v \propto \sqrt{T}$ (absolute temperature); speed rises about 0.61 m/s per $^\circ C$ near room temperature.
Speed of sound is greater in moist air.

formulas.meaning: Transverse wave on a string: T tension, $\mu$ mass per unit length
Speed of sound in a gas (Laplace)
Longitudinal wave in a solid rod

topics.neet_tip: Typical questions use the ratio of speeds in two gases or at two temperatures, and string speed when tension or diameter changes.

topics.explanation: A sinusoidal wave travelling along +x is $y(x,t) = a\sin(kx-\omega t+\phi)$. Here a is amplitude, $k = 2\pi/\lambda$ is the angular wave number, and $\omega = 2\pi\nu$ is the angular frequency. If x and t have the same sign, as in $(kx+\omega t)$, the wave travels along -x. Wave speed is $v = \omega/k$, the ratio of the coefficient of t to the coefficient of x. Particle velocity is $\partial y/\partial t$, with maximum value $a\omega$; this is different from wave speed. Particle velocity also equals $-v$ times the slope $\partial y/\partial x$. Two points separated by a path difference $\Delta x$ have phase difference $\Delta\phi = \frac{2\pi}{\lambda}\Delta x$. Two instants separated by $\Delta t$ at the same point have phase difference $\frac{2\pi}{T}\Delta t$. Intensity is proportional to $a^2\omega^2$.
key_points: $kx-\omega t$ means motion along +x; $kx+\omega t$ means motion along -x.
$v = \omega/k$ = coefficient of t divided by coefficient of x.
Maximum particle speed is $a\omega$, not v.
Phase difference = $(2\pi/\lambda) \times$ path difference.
Intensity is proportional to $a^2\omega^2$.

formulas.meaning: Particle velocity in terms of wave speed and slope

topics.neet_tip: NEET gives a wave equation and asks for v, λ, ν, direction, maximum particle speed, or phase difference between two points.
topics.topic: Displacement relation for a progressive wave

topics.explanation: Principle of superposition: when two or more waves overlap, the resultant displacement at any point is the algebraic (vector) sum of the individual displacements, $y = y_1+y_2$. Each wave then continues unaffected. For two waves of the same frequency with amplitudes $a_1$ and $a_2$ and phase difference $\phi$, the resultant amplitude is $A = \sqrt{a_1^2+a_2^2+2a_1a_2\cos\phi}$. Constructive interference occurs at $\phi = 2n\pi$, giving $A = a_1+a_2$. Destructive interference occurs at $\phi = (2n+1)\pi$, giving $A = |a_1-a_2|$. On reflection from a rigid boundary (fixed end, or a denser medium), the wave suffers a phase change of $\pi$, so the pulse is inverted. On reflection from a free end (rarer medium), there is no phase change. Frequency never changes on reflection. For an incident wave $y_i = a\sin(kx-\omega t)$ reflected at a rigid end at x = 0, the reflected wave is $y_r = a\sin(kx+\omega t)$, so that $y_i + y_r = 2a\sin kx\cos\omega t$ with a node at x = 0. NCERT writes $y_r = a\sin(kx+\omega t+\pi)$ only to illustrate the $\pi$ phase change.
key_points: Superposition holds for small, linear disturbances.
Intensity is proportional to $A^2$; $I_{max}/I_{min} = \left(\frac{a_1+a_2}{a_1-a_2}\right)^2$.
Rigid end or denser medium: phase change $\pi$ (path change $\lambda/2$).
Free end or rarer medium: no phase change.
Reflection changes direction, and possibly phase, but not frequency or speed.

formulas.meaning: Resultant amplitude of two superposed waves

topics.neet_tip: Expect resultant amplitude or intensity ratio questions, and phase change on reflection at fixed or free ends.
topics.topic: Principle of superposition and reflection of waves

topics.explanation:
Two identical waves moving in opposite directions superpose to form a standing wave, $y = 2a\sin kx\cos\omega t$. Nodes (zero amplitude) and antinodes (amplitude 2a) alternate. Adjacent nodes are $\lambda/2$ apart, and a node and the next antinode are $\lambda/4$ apart. No net energy is transported. For a string fixed at both ends, the ends are nodes, so $L = n\lambda/2$ and $
u_n = nv/2L$; all harmonics are present. For an open pipe, both ends are displacement antinodes, so $
u_n = nv/2L$ and all harmonics are present. For a closed pipe, the closed end is a node and the open end an antinode, so $
u = (2n-1)v/4L$ and only odd harmonics are present. The lowest frequency is the fundamental, or first harmonic; the fundamental of a closed pipe is half that of an open pipe of the same length. End correction is $e = 0.3d$ (0.6r) per open end.
key_points: Node-to-node distance is $\lambda/2$; node-to-antinode is $\lambda/4$.
String and open pipe: all harmonics, in the ratio 1:2:3.
Closed pipe: only odd harmonics, in the ratio 1:3:5.
In the pth harmonic of an open pipe there are p displacement nodes.
In the pth (odd) harmonic of a closed pipe there are (p+1)/2 nodes, counting the closed end.
A string fixed at both ends in the nth harmonic has n+1 nodes (including the ends) and n antinodes.
Pressure nodes are located at displacement antinodes, and vice versa.

formulas.meaning: Harmonics of a string fixed at both ends, n = 1, 2, 3, ...
Open organ pipe with end correction
Closed organ pipe, odd harmonics only

topics.neet_tip: Very high-yield: harmonic number, node/antinode counting, and comparing open and closed pipes (for example, the third harmonic of a closed pipe equal to the fundamental of an open pipe).
topics.topic: Standing waves in strings and organ pipes; fundamental mode and harmonics

topics.explanation:
When two sound waves of slightly different frequencies $
u_1$ and $
u_2$ superpose, the loudness rises and falls periodically. This is called beats. The resultant is $y = 2a\cos(\pi\Delta
u\, t)\sin(2\pi
u_{av}t)$. The tone heard has frequency $
u_{av} = (
u_1+
u_2)/2$, and its amplitude varies at the beat frequency $|
u_1-
u_2|$. The ear can distinguish beats only up to about 10 per second. Beats are used to find an unknown frequency and to tune instruments. Loading a tuning fork with wax lowers its frequency, while filing its prongs raises it. If loading the unknown fork reduces the beat count, it was the higher-frequency fork. If loading increases the beat count, it was the lower-frequency fork. Strings can be tuned the same way by changing tension.
key_points: Beat frequency = $|\nu_1-\nu_2|$.
Beat period = $1/|\nu_1-\nu_2|$.
Beats are audible only if the difference is about 10 Hz or less.
Waxing lowers a fork's frequency; filing raises it.
The unknown frequency is $\nu = \nu_{known} \pm b$; the sign is decided by the wax or file test.

formulas.meaning: Frequency of the sound actually heard

topics.neet_tip: NEET tests the wax/file sign decision, beats between two pipes or strings, and beat frequency from two given wave equations.

common_traps: Confusing particle velocity with wave velocity: maximum particle speed is $a\omega$, while wave speed is $\omega/k$. These are different quantities, linked by $v_p = -v\,\partial y/\partial x$, so $v_{p,max}/v = ak$ (the maximum slope of the wave).
Taking the frequency of KE or PE oscillation as ν: energies in SHM oscillate at $2\nu$, with period T/2.
Thinking the period of a spring-mass system changes with g or on the Moon: it depends only on m and k, whereas a pendulum's period depends on g.
Assuming a closed pipe has all harmonics: it has only odd harmonics, and its 'second overtone' is the 5th harmonic, not the 3rd.
Believing pressure changes the speed of sound: at constant temperature $P/\rho$ is constant, so v depends only on temperature, molar mass and humidity.
Counting nodes wrongly: in pipes, the open end is a displacement antinode and the closed end is a node; draw the pattern before counting.
Getting the wax/file logic backwards: wax lowers frequency, filing raises it; check whether the beat count increases or decreases.
Forgetting the small-angle condition for $T = 2\pi\sqrt{l/g}$, or measuring l only up to the top of the bob instead of to its centre.
quick_revision: Velocity leads displacement by $\pi/2$; acceleration leads displacement by $\pi$.
$T = 2\pi\sqrt{m/k}$ for a spring and $T = 2\pi\sqrt{l/g}$ for a pendulum; neither depends on amplitude.
K = U at $x = A/\sqrt{2}$; energies oscillate at twice the motion's frequency.
The x-v graph of SHM is an ellipse, becoming a circle when $\omega = 1$.
Seconds pendulum: T = 2 s, l is about 1 m; use $g_{eff}$ in accelerating frames.
Sound in air is longitudinal; transverse mechanical waves need rigidity.
In $y = a\sin(kx-\omega t)$, $v = \omega/k$ and the wave moves along +x.
Fixed end: phase change $\pi$; free end: no phase change.
Open pipe and string: all harmonics, $nv/2L$; closed pipe: odd harmonics, $(2n-1)v/4L$.
Beats = $|\nu_1-\nu_2|$, audible only up to about 10 per second; wax lowers frequency, filing raises it.
